query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal aging at intermediate temperatures induces enhanced L12 ordering in the FCC domains of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA, accompanied by the development of jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries that locally increase elastic modulus and APBE. This localized stiffness restricts cross-slip and promotes planar slip, producing stress concentrations at phase boundary tips that trigger brittle behavior. At higher temperatures, decreased ordering and the formation of more ductile transition zones along phase boundaries restore toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA in as-cast state (FCC + B2 phases)
generation.intervention: Thermal aging treatments at ~600°C (to induce maximum ordering and jagged phase boundaries) and ~750°C (to observe ordering suppression and ductile recovery)
generation.conditions: Aging performed within the 550–750°C range where chemical ordering kinetics and phase boundary evolution are pronounced; comparisons with conventional alloys under similar conditions control for grain-boundary segregation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced L12 ordering in FCC domains coupled with the formation of jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries
generation.mechanism: Increased ordering elevates the elastic modulus and APBE in the ordered domains, which restricts dislocation cross-slip, forcing planar slip. The jagged phase boundaries introduce stress concentrations that serve as initiation sites for cracks, leading to plastic instability and embrittlement. At higher aging temperatures (~750°C), reduced ordering and the development of more ductile phase boundary zones allow for improved slip transfer and toughness restoration.
generation.predicted_outcome: A non-monotonic ductile–brittle–ductile transition: maximum embrittlement (minimal toughness) is observed after aging at ~600°C, while aging at ~750°C leads to recovery of ductility. This behavior contrasts with conventional alloy embrittlement, where toughness degradation is driven primarily by grain-boundary segregation and precipitation.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys where embrittlement is controlled by grain-boundary segregation and brittle precipitation rather than by chemical ordering or phase boundary morphology
generation.boundary: Temperature regimes: below ~550°C (minimal ordering; baseline toughness), 550–750°C (brittle window driven by ordering and jagged phase boundaries), and above ~750°C (ductility recovery due to reduced ordering and formation of ductile phase boundary zones)
generation.uncertainty: While the role of L12 ordering and jagged phase boundaries is supported by mechanistic reasoning, quantifying their effects on APBE and elastic modulus—and thus on dislocation behavior—remains uncertain without direct measurements.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct thermal aging experiments on as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples at ~600°C and ~750°C. Use high-resolution TEM or TKD to image phase boundaries and quantify L12 ordering in the FCC domains. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness or impact tests) to establish ductility trends. In parallel, use conventional alloy samples aged under similar conditions as a control, ensuring impurity levels remain constant. The experiment focuses on detecting dislocation pile-ups and crack initiation at the jagged phase boundary tips, and correlating these with changes in local mechanical properties.
measurements: Microscopic evaluation (TEM/TKD) for L12 ordering and characterization of B2/FCC phase boundaries
Mechanical tests assessing toughness, dislocation behavior, and ductility
Measurements of local modulus and APBE in the ordered domains
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments reveal no significant correlation between the degree of L12 ordering/jagged phase boundary formation and the observed drop in toughness at ~600°C—specifically, if embrittlement occurs without the presence of these structural features, or if conventional alloys show similar results under identical conditions—the hypothesis will be falsified.
